display_name: Tyrrell's Vat 1 Semillon, New South Wales
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Vat 1 Semillon is Tyrrell's archetypal Hunter white — a tank-fermented, low-alcohol Semillon grown on classic Hunter soils and built to age. Its combination of sandy alluvial loam fruit and an unoaked, bottle-age development trajectory is what separates it from many modern, oak-driven whites.",
  "wine_summary": "This Vat 1 bottling matters because it is an uninterrupted expression of Hunter Valley Semillon: restrained alcohol (historic bottlings show 11.5–12% ABV), high acid clarity in youth and a distinct lane toward lanolin, honey and toast with bottle age. Tyrrell's has long positioned this wine as a pure, site-driven Semillon rather than an aromatic blend; that conservatism in winemaking lets the region's soils and the vine's natural texture do the talking. The wine's critical recognition — TEXSOM silver (2013) and gold (2016) — tracks with the Hunter practice of rewarding ageable, mineral-driven dry Semillon rather than immediate plushness.",
  "terroir_expression": "Hunter Valley's warm, humid maritime climate, punctuated by summer storm events and moderated by proximity to the coast and the Hunter River, gives Semillon thin skins and bright acidity; the vineyard soils listed for the GI — sandy alluvial loam, deep friable loam, volcanic basalt pockets and black silty loam over alkaline clay — supply both drainage and a mineral backbone. The sandy alluvial sites produce bright lemon and lanolin notes in youth, while vines on deeper friable loam and basalt contribute weight that becomes beeswax and honey as the wine evolves in bottle.",
  "vinification_summary": "Vat 1 is typically fermented with neutral handling — stainless steel or neutral vessels and minimal new oak — and bottled relatively early to preserve acidity and primary citrus notes; avoiding malolactic conversion (which would soften acidity) is a deliberate choice to retain the wine's tensile structure. That restrained vinification is the technical reason the wine ages into honeyed, toasty textures rather than extracting oak spice or overt tropical fruit.",
  "food_pairing": "Raw Sydney rock oysters with lemon — the wine's bright acid and saline minerality cut oyster brine and refresh the palate. Fried chicken with lemon mayo (casual) — low alcohol and firm acidity balance fat while allowing aged Semillon's lanolin and honey notes to play against crunchy batter. Chicken liver pâté on toasted brioche (bistro/fine) — the wine's waxy texture and developing honeyed notes harmonize with pâté richness without being overpowered. Dover sole meunière with brown butter and parsley (fine dining) — acid brightens fish and the wine's eventual nutty, toasty tertiary notes echo brown-butter aromatics. Soft-ripened goat cheese with preserved lemon — acidity cuts creaminess and the wine's citrus-lanolin spectrum complements the preserved lemon's tang.",
  "comparable_wines": "Brokenwood ILR Reserve Semillon — another Hunter benchmark that shares Vat 1's lean citrus core, lowish alcohol and extended ageability. Mount Pleasant Elizabeth Semillon — comparable for its site concentration and a similar trajectory from lemon and lanolin toward honeyed, toasty tertiary flavors with cellaring.",
  "style_profile": "Dry Semillon — light-to-medium-bodied with bright acidity and a waxy lanolin-to-honey developmental arc.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 3–25 years from vintage; store at 12–14°C on its side, away from light and vibration. Earlier drinking showcases citrus and lanolin; extended cellaring brings honeyed, toasty complexity.",
  "value_assessment": "$60. At roughly $60 retail (Wally's listings for the 2015), Vat 1 sits in the same price band as Brokenwood ILR Reserve ($50–70) and some Mount Pleasant bottlings ($45–80). It is worth the price for buyers who value provenance and long-term bottle development rather than immediate fruit; you pay for a classic Hunter Semillon profile that rewards patience.",
  "market_position": "Restaurants that list cellar-driven Australian whites, boutique wine shops and collectors who follow Hunter Semillon favor this wine. In practice it appears on classic Australian wine lists and in retail specialty tiers where buyers seek ageworthy whites rather than high-octane New World aromatics.",
  "insider_take": "Buy this if you want a wine that transforms in bottle from lemon-bright to honeyed and textural; skip it if you want instant tropical fruit or oak spice. Many consumers mistake youthful thinness for low quality — the real point of Vat 1 is how rewarding the 8–20 year evolution can be, not its immediate drinkability.",
  "aging_potential_years": 30,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 3,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 30,
